_comment: LOCAL pronunciation fixes: a replacement that applies to ONE paragraph and
nowhere else. This is the right unit for this engine.
A global rule cannot work here, and three days proved it: the model reads the
same word differently depending on what surrounds it, so a respelling that
rescues one paragraph creates a fault in another — and every such change sends
Peggy back to audio she had already approved. Vancouver is read correctly in
some paragraphs and as 'Vancouveer' in others. There is nothing to generalise.
"where" is a substring of the paragraph, matched case-insensitively — the same
kind of needle as --reroll. "replace" is applied ONLY inside that paragraph.
The source YAML is never touched: this changes what the engine hears, never
These survive regeneration. Add a line when you hear a fault, and it stays
fixed without any risk to the rest of the report.

countries/CAN/fr.where: Le Canada occupe près de 10 millions
countries/CAN/fr.why: read as Vancouveer in this paragraph; correct elsewhere

countries/CAN/fr.where: Le Canada se réchauffe à environ deux fois
countries/CAN/fr.why: the engine reads the hyphen in a year range as "moins"

Youconds sounds its final consonant HERE. Saskatchewan is NOT overridden: Sasskatchouane is a long-established global rule (2026-08-16) because French voices almost never read the name correctly — that one is not context-dependent.
81 read as "quatre-vingt-T-un" — a phantom liaison every model makes, including in Fish Audio directly. Dropping the silent gt removes the consonant it was latching onto. Peggy's suggestion.
read as English here; the -au spelling keeps the French nasal

read as "quatre contre trin" — the engine ran contre into un. The elision forces the break. This one is not optional: it stops the sentence being understood, unlike a soft Métis.
81 came out "80t'un" again; 2031 was read "deux mille trente… et un" with a pause before et un, so it is spelled hyphenated. PIB is now a GLOBAL rule.

Note this is a different failure from the parenthesis INTONATION problem, where dashes made no difference: here the nesting is what the engine cannot climb out of.

countries/USA/fr.why: Peggy pasted this paragraph into Fish Audio and Lucas read every figure correctly — from the DIGITS. Our pipeline was sending the spelled-out forms, and "deux virgule vingt-six" is where it broke. So this paragraph sends exactly what she tested. The global decimal rule stays: it earned its place on 82,16 / 80,03, and this is one paragraph, not a policy.

countries/USA/fr.where: Le réchauffement observé est plus rapide
countries/USA/fr.why: the plural s of contigus was sounded; and 1901 came out "mille neuf cen-T-un" — Peggy's respelling drops the t the engine was liaising from. Speech only, the page keeps both spellings.

countries/USA/fr.where: Projections, chacune liée à son scénario
countries/USA/fr.why: four separate faults. 1851-1900 came out HALF-CONVERTED — "mille huit cent cinquante-et-un-1900" — because the ends-in-1 rule fired on 1851 before the range rule could reach the pair, so the range rule no longer recognised it. "m" was read as the letter. "2002 augmente" gave a Z liaison. And the two scenario names kept a bare hyphen, which reads as "moins" — a comma, as for every other range.

100/20 was read "cent vingtième". It is a download/upload pair, said "cent sur vingt" in French — Peggy was unsure and suggested "100, 20"; this is the idiomatic reading of a broadband spec, and one paragraph to change if she prefers hers.
